metadata.title: Cathie Wood Buys More SpaceX Amid Tesla Merger Talks — Ron Baron Says SpaceX Could Make $50B A Year From One Data Center

content.text:
Ron Baron says SpaceX could build a $35B AI hub in under eight months and collect over $50B in annual rent.
ARK bought 37,788 SpaceX shares on Wednesday after adding 553,506 last week. It also bought 317,053 Anthropic shares.
Merz also flagged dilution from SpaceX's pledge of one new share per active Trump Account.
Cathie Wood's ARK Investment Management bought another 37,788 SpaceX shares on Wednesday as the company weighs an all-stock merger with Tesla, while billionaire investor Ron Baron said that a single SpaceX AI data center could bring in more than $50 billion a year in rent.
ARK's latest SPCX buy follows the 553,506 shares its funds bought last week. On Wednesday, the funds also bought 317,053 shares of Anthropic (ANT), SpaceX's largest AI customer.
Meanwhile, Tesla influencer Alexandra Merz sees an edge for SpaceX in the merger talks since the banks advising it already helped price its shares and lent it money.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley helped take SpaceX (SPCX) public in June. Last week, Goldman and Apollo priced $44 billion in financing for Nvidia chips and other equipment that SpaceX plans to lease. Now, Goldman and Morgan Stanley are reportedly advising SpaceX on how many of its shares to offer Tesla (TSLA) investors in a potential all-stock deal.
Baron: A $35B AI Hub Could Bring In Over $50B A Year
When Ron Baron asked a SpaceX director last month whether Elon Musk really was an incredible engineer, the director reached for a basketball comparison. "Watching Elon engineer is like watching Michael Jordan play basketball…" Baron recalled.
As of Sept. 30, Ron Baron's Baron First Principles ETF (RONB) held 40.7% of its net assets in SpaceX and 8.6% in Tesla.
On Wednesday, Baron estimated that rival developers spend about $60 billion and take 30 months on average to open a one-gigawatt data center. Specialist cloud providers rent out that capacity for $12 billion a year on long-term leases. By Baron's math, SpaceX could build a comparable site for $35 billion in under eight months and earn more than $50 billion in annual rent, even on renewable leases as short as six months.
"Means they earn their entire data center investment in eight months!!!!" Baron said. Musk warned last weekend that delays can be costly across the industry. Even a few months between paying for chips and getting them ready for paying customers, he said, could leave AI companies needing hundreds of billions of dollars in extra working capital.
Anthropic Rents Computing Power Grok Could Use Next
Anthropic (ANT) expects its monthly bill from SpaceX's AI unit to reach about $3.1 billion once it receives all the computing capacity it ordered. The Claude developer expects full delivery in December, according to its IPO prospectus. This works out to $37.2 billion a year across several agreements. Total spending could reach $120.5 billion through 2029, though either side can cancel with 90 days' notice after the initial commitments expire in January and March 2027.
Baron expects SpaceX to use more of the computing power it now rents to customers to run its own Grok models. He also expects Tesla's Full Self-Driving software and Optimus robots to drive demand for those data centers. "Anthropic is the leader in coding digital ai. We believe Grok will be the leader in physical ai due to its engineering expertise in materials, cars, rockets, robots and material science," he said.
Why A TSLA Influencer Thinks SpaceX Has Edge
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are reportedly advising SpaceX directors Roelof Botha and Randy Glein, while Evercore is advising Tesla Chair Robyn Denholm and directors Kathleen Wilson-Thompson and Jack Hartung. The two companies are worth $3.5 trillion combined. The question for negotiators is how many SpaceX shares Tesla holders would get for each share they own.
Alexandra Merz, CEO of L&F Investor Services and known on X as @TeslaBoomerMama, said on X that SpaceX's bankers know its finances firsthand. "They led its IPO. They lent it money. That is a real strength for SpaceX holders, and something Tesla holders should keep in mind," she said.
Evercore and Denholm have negotiated together before. In 2016, after Evercore reviewed SolarCity's finances, Tesla cut its offer from a range of 0.122 to 0.131 Tesla shares per SolarCity share to 0.110. Merz sees the assignment in reverse this time. "In 2016 Evercore helped Tesla pay less. In 2026 it has to help Tesla holders get more: the best exchange ratio the facts can support," she said.
What Tesla Shareholders Could Get In A SPCX-TSLA Deal
Merz wants Tesla's directors to remember what happened at Dell in 2018. A committee advised by Evercore accepted $109 per share. Large investors kept bargaining and got $120. She wants Tesla's committee to lead the talks, publish its valuation analysis and give shareholders other than Musk a separate majority vote. "We deserve a committee that fights for every share," she said.
Meanwhile, ARK's Cathie Wood expects Tesla holders to demand a premium. HSBC puts a 33% premium to Tesla's 30-day average at $507 per share. Gary Black, managing director of The Future Fund, estimates a 25% premium would put Tesla at $481 but warns an all-stock bid could send SpaceX below $100. JPMorgan sees a potential upside for SpaceX if a merger speeds its entry into the S&P 500 and draws index-fund buyers.
Merz said SpaceX's gift to children could also figure in the Tesla talks. "New share issuance is an important detail in the current merger negotiation and will be considered by the Special Committees," she said.
SpaceX pledged on Wednesday to issue one new Class A share for every active Trump Account, a tax-advantaged investment account for children. Musk will match the gift from his own holdings, so only SpaceX's contribution would dilute existing shareholders. The company did not give a final share count.
How Do Retail Traders Feel About TSLA And SPCX?
On Stocktwits, retail sentiment was 'bullish' for both TSLA and SPCX, with 'low' message volume for Tesla and 'high' volume for SpaceX.
So far this year, TSLA is down 16%, while SPCX trades 6% below its June IPO price.
